(At this point, I had no idea of what village living arrangement are, although I knew villagers wouldn't have power or running water. Most families have a sleeping house, with a separate "bush kitchen". Any showers are communal, drinking water comes from a stream or open well or a common standpipe. Typically, the bush is the toilet.)

Two children doing dishes in front of a small sink with one tap protruding from the wall above it.

A peek into our small kitchen, complete with propane stove and cold running water. ©1987, photo by S. Combs.

I make 55,000 vatu/mn (CAN$670) and CUSO gives Holly 30,000 vt or CAN$365 every month. I also get the house and utilities provided.

Lakatoro is really nice, although it's not a little native village sitting on a white sandy beach where I could take a dip before breakfast, like I envisioned. It's a collection of about 50 government houses, mostly concrete like ours (but a few made of bush materials, i.e. woven bamboo walls with natangura (sago palm) thatch, a school, some offices, and a small store (everything behind counter - two more stores are at Norsup, 8 km north) and a bank (one small room with a counter to the outside and a small floor safe inside). The buildings are set on the side of a hill and we are on the top edge, just where the deepest, darkest, jungle starts. All the grass under the trees is mowed, so it looks like a big park. There are lots of shrubs that are houseplants in Canada and coconut palms. Near our house is sugar cane, grapefruit, limes, mangoes, papaya, mandarin oranges, bananas, and sour oranges. I've been trying to find out which ones we have picking rights on - so far we're OK on the citrus trees, the papayas, the sugar cane, and the mangoes (although the season is finished on those).

Anyway, I think we'll be quite comfortable. We hung the mosquito nets last night - all the windows are well screened. We have our share of ants, but no geckos or lizards yet - nowhere to hide yet. A couple of big cockroaches last night. Rat droppings

Yale

The chronicles of such societies stretch far back in Yale’s timeline, dating back to the early 18th century. The formation of these societies seems almost inevitable considering Yale’s ethos of encouraging intellectual curiosity, even when it brushed against the conventions of the time.

But what lies beneath the surface of these secretive organizations? What mysteries and traditions have been passed down through the generations? Let’s delve deeper into the history of secret societies at Yale.

Early Beginnings of Secret Societies

Yale University has a long-standing tradition of secret societies dating back to its first establishment in 1832. These clandestine clubs, shrouded in mystery, may not be widely known, but they boast a remarkable roster of alumni who have gone on to become influential public leaders.

In the past, there were seven senior societies, and an event known as Tap Day used to be a highly publicized spectacle. During Tap Day, the junior class would gather in Branford courtyard, eagerly watching as representatives from these secret societies would dash around the court, symbolically tapping the most distinguished members of the junior class for membership.

Although this public ritual ceased in 1952, the secret societies at Yale still emerge from their cryptic meeting places, which are often windowless buildings constructed exclusively for their gatherings, every April. During this time, they engage in unique and unconventional public displays to introduce their newly chosen members to the world.

Over the years, the tradition of “tapping” has evolved. What was once a single evening of membership offers and initiation ceremonies has transformed into a more intricate process. This process now includes interviews, pre-taps, and extended initiation periods, often spanning several weeks. This extended timeline gives rising seniors ample opportunity for speculation and anticipation before the much-anticipated Tap Night finally arrives.

Evolution and Influence Over the Years

Over the years, these secret societies evolved from purely clandestine entities into potent incubators of leadership, fostering many Yale students who went on to hold prominent positions in society. They gained a reputation as an integral part of the Yale experience, helping shape the academic and cultural landscape of the institution itself.

But what was it about these societies that made them so influential? It wasn’t just the secrecy but also the bonds formed within their hallowed halls. Members of these societies forged lifelong connections, supporting and challenging each other in their personal and professional endeavors.

Exploring ten real-world examples of triangular prisms throws light on their versatility across different segments of the world. Read on to find out more!

1. Swing/slide

Swings and slides are the most essential rides at any playground. Children love swinging and sliding because of the amount of fun it gets them. The swing is usually connected to a sturdy frame and each frame houses two swings. when you carefully observe a swing frame, you can identify two triangular frames on both the right and left sides. These triangular frames provide structural strength to the swing frame.

As a result, the swing frame takes on the shape of a triangular prism when you consider the combination of these triangular sides and the rectangular faces in the front, back, and base. The triangular sides contribute to the prism’s overall structure, making it a practical example of a triangular prism in real life.

On the other hand, the slide has a ladder and a surface on which children slide and both are rectangular in shape. The ladder and the sliding surface together form a triangular prism. 

2. Ramp structures for wheelchair access

For inclusivity, some architectural designs consist of triangular ramps so that wheelchair-bound people have no issues with accessibility to buildings. While conventional ramps are not triangular prism-shaped, modern-day ramps are constructed in this manner due to better grip and increased graduality in ascent or descent. 

3. A-frame houses

A-frame houses are distinctive not only due to their name but also due to their appearance. The A-frame mimics the frame line of a triangular prism. Besides the aesthetic appeal, an A-frame house can easily shed off residues of rain and snow, eliminating the need to manually clean it. The steep roof also promotes energy efficiency by making it easy to install solar panels. 

4. Chocolate candy bars (Toblerone) 

Standing out in the supermarket for its intriguing structure is the Toblerone chocolate with its triangular prism-shaped wrapper. The wrapper contains several tiny peaks and valleys, with each peak and valley signifying a block of chocolate, making it easy for you to break off the chocolate while consuming. It is not just candy, but it’s a lot of cocoa with some math!

Peddler One will be able to squeeze in next to a set of two helicoptors. The second floor of the building has research labs, and the first floor has offices – it is a biology firm that studies the desert wildlife. The staff there will be bewildered, but will allow you through once they realize who you are.

Exiting through the front door, the squad should cross to the right side of the street, as the road on that side heads out of town and thus there will be no cars in the way. The sidewalk along the “bottom” road leading further into the city is made of concrete tiles that rarely show cracks or flaws. Street lamps – with carefully-planned gaps in-between - hang over the pavement, casting limited but brilliant yellow light onto the darkening streets that are otherwise only illuminated by the setting orange sun and the faint moon on the horizon. Cover comes in the form of the occasional bench, tall concrete embankments, or railing (as the walkway is double-tiered).
